thread.title: The Dark Side Of The Mountain

author: Eric Parnell, CFA
title: The Dark Side Of The Mountain
text:
Technology stocks are on top of the world . Whereas much of the rest of the stock market appears stuck in the mud, the information technology sector continues to climb. We haven't seen such an ascent in the technology sector since the good old days roughly two decades ago. How much longer can the tech sector keep it up? And what fate lies on the other side of the mountain top?
Exceptional performance by any measure . Technology sector results remain extraordinary by so many measures. Tech stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 Index by a nearly four-to-one margin so far in the first four and a half months of 2018. The sector has also doubled the market return over the last three years dating back to the summer of 2015. It is higher since the most recent January 29 peak whereas the rest of the market is still lower. Tech stocks now make up more than one quarter of the entire stock market by market cap. And the sector currently boasts net profit margins well in excess of +20% according to FactSet Research. Absolutely breathtaking results to be certain.
The perils of climbing to such great heights . It is said that at the summit of Mount Everest that only a third of the normal oxygen is in the air. According to the BBC , young climbers sport a 2.2% chance of dying over the average duration of their two-month Mount Everest trek, while older climbers face a notably higher 25% probability of death. Both of these odds, of course, are vastly higher than the average probability of mortality during our typical day to day closer to sea level over the same time period. Lastly and perhaps most importantly, the most dangerous part of the journey is not the climb to the peak, but instead is the descent back down from the summit into the " death zone ".
Of mountains and markets . So why all the talk about technology stocks and Mount Everest? Because the climb in technology stocks is dangerous enough at this point, particularly for retirees that can ill afford to see their capital put at great risk. But given the heights that this still ascending area of the market has reached, it is the danger that lies on the other side of the mountain that could prove terminal to many investment portfolios before it is all said and done.
It is getting harder for tech stocks to breathe . As mentioned before, the technology sector currently makes up more than one quarter of the entire U.S. stock market as measured by the S&P 500 Index (NYSEARCA: SPY ) at 25.62% to be exact. Taking this one step further, I would contend that Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN ) is a technology stock currently in consumer discretionary sector clothing (it's worth noting that it makes up a lusty 21.49% of the entire XLY ). Throw AMZN into the tech sector mix and this number goes to 28.35%.
Why does this heavy concentration in one single market sector matter? Because only one other sector has made up more than 20% of the market over the past three decades. That was financial stocks back in the mid 2000s. And we all know how well that turned out with the "financial crisis" that soon followed, as investors had to wait more than a decade to get their money back on a dividend adjusted basis on a principal value that is still lower by more than -25% to date. A deadly outcome for a retiree or near retiree to be certain.
Of course, this is not the first foray by technology stocks into the five-mile-high club either. In fact, technology stocks hold the dubious distinction of being the only sector to make up more than 25% of total stock market capitalization. The first time they did so was back in 2000 when they briefly soared as high as more than one-third of the entire market. And here we are for a second time with technology today.
The descent down tech stock mountain may prove deadly once again . The last time that technology stocks made up more than 25% of total market cap, they eventually went on to lose more than -75% of their value over the next decade. This is worse than Dow Jones Industrial Average during the Great Depression kind of stuff. Breathtakingly deadly to be certain.
Maybe this time is different, but then again... With technology stocks trading today at historically high valuations with record high profit margins, maybe this time is not going to be different. Perhaps the magnitude of the decline may not be as deep, and the duration of the decline may not be as long. But nowhere in this discussion are we considering the continued ascent into the stratosphere from current elevations. Instead, we are questioning the various degrees of likely death that lie ahead.
But what about the invincibility of the tech leaders? Ah yes. What about the five technology Clydesdales (I'm counting AMZN in this mix) that continue to lead this march higher?
This legendary handful of stocks - Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ), Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), Amazon, and Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ) - hold the distinction of also being the five largest companies in the S&P 500, making up 14.76% of its total market cap.
This is more than the second largest sector in financials in its entirety at 14.65%.
This is also more than the energy, materials, utilities, and real estate sectors combined at 14.61%.
This is not the tech sector as a whole. Instead, this is a small handful of five stocks that make up the tech sector (or are tech sector adjacent).
This is stock market concentration at its absolute worst.
And this doesn't even include the other highly speculative, tech related companies the likes of Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ) and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ) that are also riding this latest fundamentally strained technology wave.
But what about the fundamentals? To say any of these five stocks are bulletproof "nifty" is far from certain.
Yeah, I know WB from Omaha loves him some Apple (or is it Todd Combs? Or Ted Weschler? It's tougher to know exactly these days). Regardless of all of the cash on the books, a good chunk of which it set to get shipped back to shareholders, the tech behemoth remains at this time a glorified telephone maker in a shrinking product market increasingly filled with lower cost telephone makers looking to increase share with offerings that are just as technologically advanced if not superior (and more durable for that matter, just sayin'). Maybe Apple has got a next monster trick up its sleeve, but I've been seeing a lot of fourth-mover and fifth-mover disadvantages out of the company in things like smart TVs and self-driving cars from a company that lost its legendary innovation leader nearly seven years ago now. IBM (NYSE: IBM ) anyone? If anything, Apple is increasingly looking like Microsoft circa 2000 without the toll booth revenues...
Speaking of Microsoft , my nose started bleeding when I checked out its current valuation. It may have found its mojo after an extended stretch of embalming (pun intended), but at what price future growth?...
Then there's Amazon . Yes, I know the online retail giant is going to put all of my local grocery stores out of business any day now (yes, my local Whole Foods is now open, yet my local Wegman's is arguably more crowded than ever - staying long Kroger (NYSE: KR )). And yes, I know that Amazon is an ascending player in the cloud with Amazon Web Services, which still makes up a relatively meager less than 9% of total revenues, but the cloud isn't going to put my local mom-and-pop retailer out of business. In the end, Amazon is still predominantly a mega retailer that is a "money saver for everyone" as the "cheapest supply house on earth" with retail "trade that reaches around the world". Where have I heard all of this before? Oh yeah, nothing new...
Of course, we conclude our big five list with Google and Facebook , which deliver to us on a daily basis the stream of online advertisements that so many of us purposely go to great lengths to skip over or frantically navigate away from when we accidentally click on them (I know investors have historically loved to invest in companies that create products that people work to avoid). Yeah, I know the merits of AdWords and targeted advertising. I also have come to even better understand the true extent and value for better or worse of the data that these companies are compiling from their users every nanosecond of the day. I will even grant that the valuations for these companies while rich are certainly not egregious. But I also know that technological cycles are evolving at an exponentially rapid pace. And that the way we search whatever it is that we might be searching five to ten years from now on whatever device we are using may be vastly different than what we are doing today (R.I.P. the desktop computer wars between Dell and Compaq, the phone book, the print newspaper, the flip cell phone, Netscape, and MySpace among many other things that were so popular not that long ago). And when I hear things like "nobody uses X anymore" or "I use X only when I want to get in touch with grandma", it is the same as the scent of blood in the thin mountain air...
Know that the greatest dangers for technology stocks lie ahead . Technology stocks may continue to rise to the moon. They might once again ascend to more than 35% of the entire market. Heck, they might make up more than half of the market before it's all said and done. Tech stock net profit margins may expand in excess of 30%, or +4 standard deviations above their historical mean. And Apple could become the first $5 trillion market cap company in the process. But probabilities are all heavily weighted against such outcomes.
When one climbs to the peak of Mount Everest, the question is not whether to climb even higher, because you can't. Instead, the question turns to how to safely get back down from the top of the world. Such is the challenge that is almost certain to eventually encounter tech heavy investors going forward.
Such is the long-term advantage of being a contrarian . For when so many investors eventually find themselves trapped on their way down the stock market mountainside, the contrarian is already at work capitalizing on all of the good opportunities left behind by the market along the way. And being squarely on the ground is the best way to protect the retirement savings you have worked so long and hard to accumulate.
